In this lesson, you will learn about the operation of a zener diode regulator.
INTRODUCTIONM
Regulator circuits provide a constant output voltage even when the input voltage varies or when the output current varies.
Circuit operation is based on changing the effective resistance of the circuit when input and output conditions vary.
Let's begin the lesson on ZENER DIODE REGULATOR OPERATION...................
LESSON MENU
ZENER DIODE REGULATOR CIRCUIT
This is a typical zener diode regulator circuit............
DISCUSSION
Q1 is the component that automatically changes resistance to maintain a constant Vout. Notice that Q1 is in the common base configuration.
The output voltage of a rectifier filter is applied to the collector of Q1.
The load is connected to the emitter of Q1.
Current flow is from ground, through RL and Q1, to the rectifier filter.
Current flow is from the rectifier filter to Q1, RL, and then to ground.
Since RL and Q1 are in series, this zener diode regulator is a series voltage regulator.
R1 and D1 form a voltage divider that applies base bias to Q1. Collector bias is obtained directly from the rectifier filter.
The emitter voltage is developed by the action of the transistor. Ee = Eb - .6V
The operation of this series voltage regulator is based on two principles.
Let's investigate the operation of D1 first.
Recall that a zener diode maintains a constant voltage drop as long as it is operating in the breakdown region.
For example, if the zener voltage for D1 is 6 V and if 8 V is applied, D1 conducts reverse current flow so that R1 drops 2 V, leaving 6 V on the base of Q1.'
If the input voltage increases to 9 V, D1 conducts more so that R1 drops 3 V, leaving 6 V on the base of Q1.
If the input voltage decreases to 7 V, D1 conducts less so that R1 drops 1 V, leaving 6 V on the base of Q1.
In other words, the base bias for Q1 is always 6 V as long as the DC input voltage is 6 V or greater.
Now, let's investigate the action of Q1.
With a base voltage of + 6 V, the emitter is placed at + 5.4 V.
If the input voltage is + 8V, the action of Q1 drops 2.6 V from the collector to emitter.
If the input voltage increases to 9 V, Q1 must drop 3.6 V. In effect, Q1 collector to emitter resistance increased.
If the input voltage decreases to 7 V, Q1 must drop 1.6 V. In effect, Q1 collector to emitter resistance decreased.
The result is that the output voltage, voltage on the emitter is held constant even if the input voltage varies.
Also, if the load current varies (due to a change in load resistance) the output voltage is held constant by the action of Q1..
Again, the voltage on the emitter, which is the output voltage, is established by the action of Q1.
If RL decreases, it will cause Vout (Ee) to also decrease. This will cause load current to increase. to increase because the load drops more voltage.
When Ee increases, the base to emitter PN junction forward bias decreases, increasing collector to emitter resistance. This causes Q1's collector to emitter current to decrease.
When Ee increases, the base to emitter PN junction forward bias decreases, increasing emitter to collector resistance. This causes Q1's emitter to collector current to decrease.
When Ee increases, the base to emitter PN junction forward bias decreases, increasing emitter to collector resistance. This causes Q1's emitter to collector current to decrease...
By decreasing Q1's resistance, Q1 drops less voltage (Vce), bringing Vout back up to its original output of 5.4 V.
If RL increases, this will cause Vout to also increase. This will cause load current to decrease.output of 5.4 V.
When Ee increases, the base to emitter PN junction forward bias decreases, increasing collector to emitter resistance. This causes Q1's collector to emitter current to decrease.
When Ee increases, the base to emitter PN junction forward bias decreases, increasing emitter to collector resistance. This causes Q1's emitter to collector current to decrease.
By increasing Q1's resistance, Q1 drops more voltage (Vce), taking Eout back down to its original output of 5.4 V.
"By increasing Q1's resistance, Q1 drops more voltage (Vce), taking Eout
The result is that the output voltage, (voltage on the emitter), is held constant even if the output current varies.
Putting the circuit together, D1 holds the base of Q1 at Vz and the output is held at Vz minus .6 V under varying conditions.
A negative voltage divider is constructed by reversing the diode and using a PNP transistor.

Notice Q1 on the card and schematic. Q1 is a power transistor.
Since the transistor is in series with the load, total load current flows through Q1.
